[Inkling](https://thinkingmachines.ai/inkling/) [@inkling_page] is a pair of
open-weight, multimodal foundation models from Thinking Machines Lab
(measured 2026-09-09).
This is a model release, not a coding agent or a chat product:
the weights are downloadable,
and the company's own hosted surfaces for it are a fine-tuning API
and a playground rather than an end-user assistant.
This section summarizes the release and asks whether it matters for our workflow.

#### Who Thinking Machines Lab is

Thinking Machines Lab is a San Francisco AI startup founded in February 2025
by Mira Murati, formerly OpenAI's chief technology officer,
with John Schulman, an OpenAI co-founder, as chief scientist
[@wikipedia_thinking_machines].
It raised $2 billion at a $12 billion valuation in July 2025,
and two founding members left for OpenAI in January 2026
[@wikipedia_thinking_machines].
Its first product, [Tinker](https://thinkingmachines.ai/tinker/) [@tinker_page],
released in October 2025,
is a LoRA fine-tuning API for open-weight models
where the customer writes the training loop in Python
and Thinking Machines runs the GPUs [@wikipedia_thinking_machines].
Inkling is the company's first in-house model,
released on 2026-07-15 [@inkling_announcement].

#### What Inkling is

Two models share the name (measured 2026-09-09) [@inkling_page]:

- **Inkling**: a mixture-of-experts transformer with 975 billion total parameters,
  41 billion of them active per token,
  and a context window of up to one million tokens
  [@inkling_announcement].
- **Inkling-Small**: 276 billion total parameters, 12 billion active,
  released 2026-07-30 and post-trained by on-policy distillation
  with Inkling as the teacher [@inkling_small_announcement].
  The product page says it matches the larger model on many benchmarks
  at a quarter of the size [@inkling_page].

Both accept text, image, and audio input and produce text only
[@inkling_model_card; @inkling_small_model_card].
Both are released under the Apache 2.0 license
[@inkling_model_card; @inkling_small_model_card],
and both expose an effort setting that trades reasoning tokens for score;
the reported evaluations are run at `effort=0.99` [@inkling_announcement].

The announcement positions Inkling as a broad base for customization
rather than a leaderboard winner [@inkling_announcement].
Its claims, and the evidence offered for them:

- **Breadth**: reported scores of 77.6% on SWE-Bench Verified,
  63.8% on Terminal Bench 2.1, 87.2% on GPQA Diamond,
  and 73.5% on MMMU Pro, all at the highest effort setting [@inkling_announcement].
- **Efficiency**: the company reports that Inkling matches
  NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra on Terminal Bench 2.1
  using roughly a third of the tokens [@inkling_announcement].
- **Training**: 45 trillion tokens of text, image, audio, and video,
  then supervised fine-tuning on synthetic data
  and reinforcement learning with more than 30 million rollouts [@inkling_announcement].

These are the vendor's own numbers on the vendor's own runs;
we have not reproduced any of them.
Inkling-Small's announcement reports 80.2% on SWE-Bench Verified
and 31.6% on Humanity's Last Exam,
against Inkling's 77.6% and 29.7% [@inkling_small_announcement].

#### How it is accessed and priced

Access routes (measured 2026-09-09):

- **Weights**: on Hugging Face, in BF16 and `NVFP4` checkpoints
  [@inkling_model_card; @inkling_small_model_card].
  Even the smaller model has 276 billion parameters,
  so neither fits any hardware the lab owns.
- **Tinker**: LoRA fine-tuning at 64K or 256K context,
  and a beta serverless inference endpoint,
  both billed per million tokens [@tinker_models_pricing].
  Under a limited-time 50% discount,
  fine-tuning Inkling at 64K context costs $1.87 per million prefill tokens,
  $4.68 per million sampled tokens, and $5.61 per million training tokens,
  roughly doubling at 256K;
  Inkling-Small is about a third of that.
  Serverless inference is $1.00 input and $4.05 output per million tokens
  for Inkling, and $0.30 and $1.20 for Inkling-Small.
  Checkpoint storage adds $0.10 per GB per month [@tinker_page].
- **Third-party hosts**: the announcement lists Together AI, Fireworks, Modal,
  Databricks, and Baseten as hosts,
  and vLLM, SGLang, and `llama.cpp` among supported inference engines
  [@inkling_announcement].
  Our quota-aware defaults for the Databricks endpoint are already in
  @tbl-databricks-oaicopilot-defaults.

#### What it is for

Thinking Machines' stated bet is that organizations will want to
fine-tune a capable open model on their own data
rather than rent a closed frontier model,
and Inkling exists to give Tinker a strong first-party base
[@inkling_announcement].
Tinker's own pitch lists specialized agents, forecasting,
continual learning, and AI research as the intended uses [@tinker_page].
The audio and image inputs make it a candidate
for transcription-plus-reasoning pipelines as well as coding.

#### Useful to us? Marginally, and only through a host

As a coding-agent backend,
Inkling is one more open-weight option alongside the models
in @sec-ai-catalog-coding-agents,
reachable through Databricks (@sec-ai-byok-vscode)
or, when a host lists it there, OpenRouter (@sec-ai-opencode-openrouter).
Its reported SWE-Bench and Terminal Bench scores are competitive
but not ahead of the closed models we already pay for,
and the 8,192-token output cap on the Databricks endpoint
is a real constraint for agentic edits.
Self-hosting is out: the lab has no machine
within an order of magnitude of the memory required.

The more interesting angle is research.
Tinker lets a student run a fine-tuning or reinforcement-learning experiment
on a frontier-class open model
with a Python training loop and no cluster administration,
and universities can ask for wider access [@tinker_page].
If a project ever needs to adapt a model
to epidemiological text or lab-specific coding conventions,
Tinker with Inkling-Small is a cheap place to try it.
Until such a project appears,
no action is needed beyond keeping the Databricks endpoint in our defaults table.
